extracted.intended_audience: journalists, editors, media critics, and journalism students
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and best practices for reporting serious allegations (here: campus sexual-assault feature reporting), emphasizing verification, corroboration, falsifiability, and editorial accountability. Focuses on how reporters and editors should gather, check, and present evidence before publishing high-impact claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attempt to contact alleged perpetrators / all implicated parties
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters should try to speak with the accused or other implicated individuals rather than relying solely on the victim’s account or a single intermediary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The piece argues Erdely should have tried to speak with the alleged rapists; even if they might not talk, one might get a deniable response or names to pursue. If names are found, run Web searches, call around, ask friends, and investigate any history of misconduct. The article notes Erdely said she 'reached out' in multiple ways but largely did not contact the accused.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corroborate claims with multiple sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not let a single source stand as the sole basis for a story about a serious crime; obtain more than one source and corroborating evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author criticizes allowing a waiver of 'the usual journalistic protocols, such as getting more than one source on a story about a horrible crime.' Even if a subject is deemed 'credible,' reporters and editors should still seek independent corroboration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test hypotheses; seek falsifying evidence (Popperian falsifiability)
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists should attempt to disprove or falsify their working hypotheses rather than only collecting confirming evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Drawing on Karl Popper, the article recommends actively looking for evidence that would refute the story (for example, evidence exonerating the accused). Evidence corroborates a theory best when it emerges from an attempt to falsify it; reporters should welcome and pursue disconfirming facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verify basic factual details (events, dates, presence of gatherings)
rubrics_metrics.description: Confirm the concrete, checkable facts underlying a narrative (e.g., whether a party occurred on a given night, who was present).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Rolling Stone story failed on basic checks—'there was no party at the frat house that night, no frat brother fits the description'—so journalists should verify details such as whether events took place, maps/records of the location, and who was present.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be aware of and counteract confirmation bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize and actively mitigate the tendency to seek only evidence that confirms preexisting beliefs or widely held narratives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article notes reporters and readers may be in the grip of prevailing myths (e.g., 'frat boys rape girls' or 'universities are indifferent'), which can cause selective acceptance of confirming evidence. Reporters must guard against this by seeking disconfirming information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain editorial protocols; do not waive verification for narrative or perceived credibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors should enforce standard verification procedures even when a reporter or subject appears 'credible' or the story aligns with widely held concerns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author faults editors for allowing Erdely to waive protocols; editorial standards like multiple sourcing, contacting implicated parties, and rigorous fact-checking should not be suspended because a subject seems credible or the story is sympathetic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use investigative methods to identify and vet implicated individuals
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ available investigative tools (directories, web searches, contacts, friends) to identify subjects and check their backgrounds and possible corroborating witnesses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a reporter uncovers identifying details, they should use them to find names, search online, contact acquaintances, and look for prior misconduct or corroboration, rather than leaving identities unverified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance sensitivity to victims with rigorous verification
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat alleged victims with respect and sensitivity while still pursuing independent verification and corroboration of their claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some defenders argued rigorous questioning could retraumatize victims or silence them; the article says sensitivity is important but does not excuse foregoing standard checks—rigor and empathy must coexist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider the real-world impact of reporting and act with appropriate caution
rubrics_metrics.description: Because journalism can produce immediate and far-reaching consequences, reporters and editors must weigh potential impacts and ensure claims are well-founded before publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Rolling Stone story led to major institutional responses (e.g., UVA suspending fraternities). Given such impact, the article urges heightened care in verification and sourcing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public accountability and clear ownership of errors
rubrics_metrics.description: When reporting failures occur, media organizations should acknowledge responsibility, issue clear corrections/apologies, and avoid deflecting blame onto victims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author criticizes Rolling Stone’s 'non-apology apology' that implied the victim was at fault and insists the magazine and reporter should 'own up to it.'
